rows.explainer:
We did not find much evidence on the efficacy of the PCV vaccine by dose, so this is a rough assumption based on available evidence. 

“When stratified by time since vaccination, one dose was protective for up to 6 months (84%, 58–94) but we could not show protection 6 months or more after vaccination (33%, –143 to 81). Compared with no vaccine, point estimates for effectiveness of two, three, or four doses when given on an infant schedule were close to each other, with widely overlapping CI and were more effective than a single dose (table 4). Effectiveness of two, three, and four-dose schedules was similar up to 6 months after vaccination (97% [87–99] for 2 doses, 100% [96–100] for 3 doses, and 100% [58–100] for 4 doses).” Whitney et al. 2006 
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17071283/

rows.explainer:
This is a rough assumption based on evidence regarding the relative efficacy of HiB vaccine doses (one of Penta's constituent vaccines). We were unable to find evidence on the efficacy of the overall Penta vaccine. 

“A meta-analysis of four case-control studies examined the dose-specific effect of Hib conjugate vaccines on Hib meningitis morbidity (1 dose: RR=0.64, 95% CI 0.38-1.06; 2 doses: RR=0.09, 95% CI 0.03-0.27; 3 doses: RR=0.06, 95% CI 0.02-0.22), consistent with results from single RCTs” Davis et al. 2013 
https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3847464/

One dose of HiB protected against ~38% of HiB cases 
((1 - 0.64) / (1-.006) = .383); whereas 2 doses protected against ~97% of cases ((1-0.09)/(1-0.06) = .968). This shows a similar pattern to the efficacy of the PCV vaccine (below) so we use the same rough assumptions for both.

This is a rough assumption based on evidence regarding the relative efficacy of HiB vaccine doses (one of Penta's constituent vaccines). We were unable to find evidence on the efficacy of the overall Penta vaccine. 

“A meta-analysis of four case-control studies examined the dose-specific effect of Hib conjugate vaccines on Hib meningitis morbidity (1 dose: RR=0.64, 95% CI 0.38-1.06; 2 doses: RR=0.09, 95% CI 0.03-0.27; 3 doses: RR=0.06, 95% CI 0.02-0.22), consistent with results from single RCTs” Davis et al. 2013 
https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3847464/

One dose of HiB protected against ~38% of HiB cases 
((1 - 0.64) / (1-.006) = .383); whereas 2 doses protected against ~97% of cases ((1-0.09)/(1-0.06) = .968). This shows a similar pattern to the efficacy of the PCV vaccine (below) so we use the same rough assumptions for both.

Risk of wastage: Double treatment
rows.explainer: We adjust for this elsewhere in our model.

rows.label: Risk of wastage: Ineffective goods
rows.explainer: Possibility of ineffective vaccines is adjusted for elsewhere in the model

rows.label: Goods purchased and left in storage until they expire / Cash doesn't reach recipients or is taken back from them inappropriately
rows.explainer: "Goods purchased and left in storage until they expire" is not applicable to New Incentives, which does not distribute commodities. The value of the cash itself is a very small portion of the benefits we model from New Incentives' program, so we have skipped making an adjustment to the consumption benefits for the risk of fraud. Separate from the adjustment in this row, we consider whether the risk of fraud is higher in the period following the RCT than it was during the RCT. If so, we consider adjusting how effective we expect the cash transfers to be at incentivizing vaccination.

rows.label: Total adjustment for risk of wastage
Misappropriation without monitoring results
rows.explainer: To date, New Incentives monitoring has been comprehensive of its activities.

rows.label: False monitoring results
rows.explainer: We have relatively high confidence in New Incentives' monitoring, which involves multiple rounds of checks and audits by different teams. We make a small downward adjustment to account for our having spent more total time over years of review interrogating some of our other top charities' monitoring methods, relative to a single round of intensive review of New Incentives' monitoring before adding it to our list of top charities in 2020.

rows.label: Total adjustment for quality of monitoring and evaluation
Change of priorities
rows.explainer: We do not believe that this is a meaningful risk with New Incentives, which runs a single program. Our impression from conversations with New Incentives is that it is seeking to implement the program with high fidelity to the way it was implemented during the RCT because deviations from that model could undermine New Incentives' and GiveWell's confidence that the program was continuing to have a similar level of impact.

rows.label: Confidence in funds being used for intended purpose: Non-funding bottlenecks
rows.explainer: As noted in our review of New Incentives (https://www.givewell.org/charities/new-incentives), there is a risk that government opposition to the program could reduce the impact of the program. We would guess that the risk of lost impact is small because New Incentives has been operating the program since 2017 and opposition has not yet affected impact.

rows.explainer: Not applicable: single program organization.
